question: Is it permissible for men to wear silk ties?
answer:
In response to this, our Prophet ﷺ picked up gold and silver and said that these two are permissible for the women of my Ummah and haram for the men of my Ummah. And therefore this is the verdict that has been pretty much accepted by the mainstream and the bulk of Islamic scholarship: that silk and gold are not befitting for a man to wear. And as our Prophet ﷺ said, "Whoever wears silk in this world shall not wear it in the next life." In other words, you're going to be deprived of something that is far better. Why would you not want the silks of Jannah?

The reason our scholars give for this (and this is the wisdom, not the cause): the wisdom is that it is effeminate, that it is not befitting the dignity of a man. So again, the Shariah actually does believe in something called masculinity and femininity. In our cultures and times this concept is being discarded and thrown out the window, and we're being told that there's no such thing as masculinity or being a gentleman, and there's no such thing as femininity; they're all constructs. We don't believe this. We believe there are certain characteristics that are masculine and certain characteristics that are feminine, and the two of them are complementary. So the point being that getting too involved with the fineries of this world is not befitting the dignity of a man. It is not something that looks good on a man, to be decorated top to bottom with gold and with silk and these things. So our Prophet said that this is not allowed for the men of my Ummah.

That having been said, a concession has been given. And what is that concession? The hadith is in Sahih Muslim: Umar ibn al-Khattab radiyAllahu 'anhu was giving a khutbah, and he said the Prophet ﷺ forbade us to wear silk except for two or three or four fingers. In one version he picked his hand up and went like this: except for a portion, a patch, a small bit of silk, two or three or four fingers, basically a strip. Except for this, it is allowed.

So based on this hadith, the vast majority of scholars, actually three of the four madhhabs, said that a small amount of silk that is used as decoration is allowed, for example the fringes. You have to realize that in those days they didn't have the capability to make these types of garments, with all of these different patterns woven together. If they wanted to decorate a garment, they would put a patch on it. So the garment would be a base of one thing, and then they would take maybe some silk, and maybe the embroidery would be silk, or maybe the patch would be a design patched on as silk: the decorations on the garment. These days they have all of this already woven in; you can see the exotic patterns, for example, on this particular kurta that I'm wearing. But in those days they didn't have that.

So, as I said, they would take different cloths and make the pattern. Especially, what was most common back then was the fringes, the fringes of the cuffs. In our days we have the cuff links; in those days they would have the brocade and the sash, maybe at the bottom of the thawb as well. That was also common, at the bottom of the long thawb or the shirt, and also at the ends of the sleeves they would have maybe patches of silk to make it look dignified or beautiful or whatnot. So Umar ibn al-Khattab said: except for two or three or four fingers. Based on this, therefore, if there is a small amount of silk that's for decoration purposes, that is inshaAllah acceptable.

Now, when it comes to ties, the position that I hold, and Allah knows best: first and foremost, we have to realize that much of what passes as silk today is not actual silk. There are actually ties that say 100% silk, and what they mean is 100% synthetic silk. Because, you see, the actual silk which is prohibited is the silk of the silkworm. There is plenty of polyester, or different types of cloth or material that are different percentages of cotton and of polyester and of wool, and they try to make it feel like silk, make it silk-like, but it is not actual silk. The actual silk that is forbidden is the silk that comes from the cocoon of the silkworm. And of course that type of silk is extremely expensive, and it is laborious and painstaking. You have to get thousands of the cocoons of the silkworm and then make from them basically one garment, and it takes a lot of manual labor; even machines cannot really do that.

So what passes for silk in our times, most of it is not silk. If that is the case, you need to find out, when you see the garment and it says silk, what is it: synthetic silk or real silk? If it is synthetic silk, it is completely permissible, because this is like taking a metal and painting it the color of gold and then saying this is gold. Well, it's not gold. You can call it golden; it is not gold. And what the Shariah forbids is the actual silk. So realize this: an actual real silk tie would not be sold at your average places for an average sum; it's going to be an exorbitant amount of money. And you get plenty of polyester and plenty of good ties that are synthetic silk; it's not real silk, and it looks like silk.

As for actual silk ties, these are the very expensive ties, the name brands and whatnot. The position that I hold is that it comes under this exception that Umar ibn al-Khattab narrated from the Prophet: that he forbade silk except for two or three or four fingers. Now again, some people say, "Oh, the tie at the bottom is more than four fingers." SubhanAllah, it's not. You don't have to be that literalistic. The point is that an embellishment or a decoration that is a strip is something that is permitted. And this is the position that I hold: that a pure silk tie, an actual silk tie, would come under this, because it is a strip and it is meant as embellishment.

Now somebody says it is a separate strip. The response is that with the technicalities here, I think you're getting lost in the point. The point is that what is forbidden would be a silk shirt, let's say, a silk suit, a silk jacket, a complete silk jacket. And by the way, if there's a percentage of silk in it, inshaAllah less than 30%, for example, this would be permissible. Because 30%, that would be where it gets problematic; anything less than 30% can be overlooked, because the majority would not be silk. But if it is a pure silk tie, in my opinion it does not come under the prohibition in the first place. Nonetheless, if you feel that it did, it is your prerogative, in which case you follow the other position and choose other ties in that regard.

As for this notion that the tie itself is not allowed because it is a symbol of Christianity or whatnot, this is a myth. It has no basis in reality, in the sense that nobody ever wore a tie that was meant to be an indication of a theology. Nobody has done that, and it is not done anymore. So this is complete mythology.

So it is completely permissible to dress like the cultures of your time and place, as in fact our Prophet ﷺ himself dressed, and dressed up, in accordance with the culture of his time and place. I've talked about this in other lectures. When our Prophet ﷺ dressed up, according to what culture was he dressing up? It was the culture of pre-Islam, the culture of the Arabs that existed before the coming of Islam. Our Prophet ﷺ did not change the cultural statements; he did not bring a fashion revolution. So when he dressed, he dressed like the people of his time; when he dressed up, he dressed up like the people of his time.

And this indicates that the default, as Ibn al-Qayyim says, the Sunnah, the real Sunnah, is to dress like your own culture dresses, as long as it is halal. In other words, the awrah has to be covered, the material has to be halal, and whatnot. Otherwise, culturally speaking, you should conform to your people as much as possible, as our Prophet ﷺ did, and as the Ummah has done throughout all of our last 14 centuries. Wherever Islam went, the peoples of those lands, when they embraced Islam, might have modified their garb or changed certain things, but in the end they dressed like their own peoples.

And that is why the Muslims of Nigeria, mashaAllah, have their colorful ways of dressing; the Muslims of Indonesia dress the way that they do; the Muslims of Afghanistan and the Muslims of Pakistan have their dress codes. Nobody said, "Oh, that is a haram dress code." So now that Muslims are in Western lands, in America and England and Canada and whatnot, we may dress like the people that we are living amongst. Completely permissible. But we have to make sure our awrah is covered, that it is loose, etc.

And the position that I hold, and Allah knows best, is that **ties are completely permissible, even if they are made out of silk**, because they come under this notion of an embellishment that is a little bit, just a strip. This is exactly the goal of this concession given. Actually, if you look at it, the sash that would have been at the bottom of a garment would probably have more silk than a simple silk tie, and it was overlooked and allowed. And Allah 'azza wa jall knows best.
